summary:
The core objective of BAT is to merge the VIIRS and MODIS records into a small, optimized and precise dataset for a web application, in order to allow the user to easily extract usable information in a visual, user-friendly environment.
Close hotspots were analyzed by time and distance, and unified into a standardized 1 km weekly grid. Rather than choosing either instrument, overlapping sub-pixel detections were joined to preserve vital physical telemetry, such as Fire Radiative Power (FRP), Flame Thermal Contrast (ΔT), and sub-pixel fire density, eliminating redundancies and reducing the global dataset by over 46%. To fix the sensitivity gap between the continuous 26-year MODIS baseline (2000–2025) and the higher-resolution VIIRS sensors (2012–2025), a seasonal cross-calibration aligns observations to a shared 2003–2023 climatological normal. This harmonized foundation drives an L₂-regularized multivariate forecasting model (F₂) that projects local fire risk anomalies one to four weeks ahead. Ultimately, BAT allows a visual approach to this pipeline through an interactive 2D and 3D web platform featuring multi-year burning calendar heatmaps, side-by-side annual comparisons, and customizable spatial queries, transforming decades of raw satellite thermal anomalies into actionable wildfire intelligence.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Brightness Anomaly Tracker is an open-access web platform for exploring, analyzing, and forecasting wildfire activity worldwide. It uses 25 years of real NASA satellite data (2000–2025), processing hundreds of millions of fire detections into a unified dataset that allows users to explore historical patterns and future activity.

The platform combines observations from NASA's satellite instruments, primarily:

  • MODIS: Available through the Terra and Aqua satellites, providing the historical foundation of the dataset from 2000 to 2025.
  • VIIRS: Available since 2012, offering higher spatial resolution and greater sensitivity to smaller and less intense fires.

All data is obtained through NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System). The platform processes and combines observations from different sensors, accounting for their differences to produce a consistent global record of fire activity. It then applies machine learning models to generate short-term forecasts, covering up to four weeks ahead.

Users can access this information through an interactive web interface featuring 3D and 2D maps, historical analysis, and fire activity forecasts. The platform also provides a documented REST API for accessing processed data and model outputs.

The platform is live and publicly accessible at https://firecalglobal.duckdns.org

How does the system work?

BAT's workflow consists of five interconnected stages, from raw satellite data collection to interactive visualization and forecasting.

  • Data Ingestion and Spatial Merge: Data is collected from the NASA FIRMS API across all countries, sensors, and available years. Quality filters based on land cover and detection confidence remove unreliable observations. The remaining records are merged into a unified 0.01° grid (approximately 1 km resolution). This process reduces duplicate records by approximately 46%, while preserving key measurements such as detection counts, fire radiative power (FRP), brightness temperatures, and daytime/nighttime activity.
  • Multi-Sensor Harmonization (M₂ Model): MODIS and VIIRS have different detection characteristics, making their raw fire counts unsuitable for direct comparison. The M₂ model corrects these differences using seasonal calibration factors across five climate zones. Trained on overlapping data from 2012–2023 and validated against independent 2025 data, it achieved a 97.87% reduction in global MAE. This produces a consistent fire activity time series covering 2000–2025.
  • Predictive Model (F₂): A Ridge L₂ regression model generates forecasts from one to four weeks ahead for 16,525 terrestrial grid points across 203 countries. It uses six features describing recent fire activity, FRP intensity, thermal contrast, nighttime detections, and subpixel density. Physical constraints guide the model to produce realistic predictions. When historical information is insufficient, the system uses F₀ (local climatology) as an alternative. The method used for each forecast is identified in both the API and the interface.
  • Backend API: A Python API provides access to processed observations, model outputs, and precomputed forecasts. Data is stored in Parquet files and accessed through PyArrow using lazy, batch-aware reads. An SQLite analytical database (approximately 542 MiB) handles aggregated queries, while a dedicated 1.5 GB F₂ cache enables sub-second responses for previously computed forecasts. The main API endpoints include map-based exploration and access to forecasts for selected countries or specific grid points, allowing users to visualize geographic data and retrieve relevant climate predictions.
  • Interactive Web Frontend: The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. It provides an interactive 3D globe using Three.js/WebGL and a 2D geographic map using D3.js, both displaying color-coded fire detections. Additional features include historical monthly activity charts (2000–2025), year-to-year comparisons, and F₂/F₀ forecast visualizations. Users can filter data by sensor, month, metric, and resolution, as well as export displayed datasets to CSV.

What benefits does it have?

BAT Global makes NASA's extensive wildfire data more accessible and useful for different audiences.

For researchers and scientists, it provides 25 years of harmonized fire activity data from multiple satellites in a single platform. This enables historical and cross-sensor analysis without requiring custom data processing pipelines. All metrics include their units, data sources, and known limitations, while training scripts, evaluation benchmarks, and model weights are publicly documented and reproducible. The M₂ model achieves a 97.87% reduction in global MAE, while F₂ improves forecasting performance over climatology by 29.47% in Brazil and 25.71% globally at the one-week horizon.

For environmental managers and policymakers, BAT offers tools to identify fire activity patterns across countries and regions, compare different years and seasons, and access forecasts up to four weeks ahead for 203 countries. These capabilities can support environmental monitoring, risk assessment, and proactive resource planning.

For the general public, the platform provides an intuitive way to explore global wildfire activity without requiring GIS expertise or technical knowledge. Its interactive 3D and 2D maps, bilingual interface (English and Portuguese), and mobile-responsive design make the information accessible from any device. BAT is completely free, requires no account or installation, and is available through any web browser.

What is the intended impact of the project?

BAT aims to democratize access to NASA's 25 years of wildfire data, transforming it into a freely accessible and practical resource. In the short term, it provides researchers, NGOs, journalists, and environmental educators with tools to analyze fire activity trends and compare different years and satellite sensors, without requiring expensive infrastructure or months of custom data processing.

In the long term, BAT can contribute to the development of early warning systems and wildfire monitoring initiatives, particularly in developing regions such as tropical South America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia. Its historical data and forecasting capabilities can also support government agencies in monitoring deforestation-related fires, land-use changes, and seasonal fire patterns.

Beyond its environmental applications, the project demonstrates that production-grade public data platforms can be built using NASA's open datasets. It also establishes a foundation for future improvements, including near-real-time satellite data integration and more advanced machine learning models. By providing a standardized and openly documented fire activity dataset, BAT enables other researchers to reproduce its results, conduct comparisons, and build upon its work.What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

BAT's technology stack was designed to handle hundreds of millions of records while maintaining reliability, low infrastructure costs, and ease of maintenance by a small team.

The main tools and technologies include:

  • Python 3.12.2: Data ingestion, ETL pipelines, machine learning, and REST API.
  • TypeScript / TSX: Frontend development using React components and hooks.
  • HCL (Terraform): Infrastructure as Code and AWS resource provisioning.
  • Bash: Deployment automation, local startup scripts, and data transfers.
  • SQL: Analytical queries using SQLite, with optional PostgreSQL support.

How is your project creative?

BAT combines scientific modeling and resource-efficient engineering to address limitations in existing wildfire data platforms.

Its M₂ harmonization model creates a consistent 25-year multi-satellite fire activity record, enabling comparisons that are not directly possible with raw MODIS and VIIRS data. The F₂ model uses physically constrained Ridge regression instead of a black-box architecture, making its predictions more interpretable and easier for domain experts to evaluate. When historical information is insufficient, a transparent F₀/F₂ hybrid approach selects local climatology as an alternative, clearly identifying the method used for each forecast.

The project also demonstrates how large-scale environmental data can be processed with limited resources. Serving approximately 296 million records on a 1 GiB RAM server for US$15/month required techniques such as lazy PyArrow reads, atomic forecast caching, and serialized heavy queries. The system passed its automated tests under a 700 MiB memory limit without out-of-memory errors.

Finally, BAT prioritizes transparency by exposing known limitations directly in the interface, including experimental forecasts, the underperforming two-week prediction horizon, and the fact that missing detections do not necessarily indicate the absence of fire. Its entire pipeline, from data ingestion and model training to deployment, is scripted, documented, and version-controlled for reproducibility.

What factors did your team consider?

The team considered scientific integrity, operational costs, security, and reproducibility throughout development.

  • Scientific integrity: Zero values were preserved rather than imputed to avoid masking coverage gaps. ISO week 53 edge cases were handled across aggregation functions, and F₂ was evaluated using an independent 2025 holdout. All forecasts are labeled experimental and are not endorsed by NASA. The team also followed NASA Space Apps AI/ML guidelines and prepared the required AI Disclosure statement.
  • Cost and sustainability: AWS RDS was avoided in favor of SQLite on EBS, keeping infrastructure costs at approximately US$15/month. A documented migration path to RDS and larger instances is available as usage grows.
  • Security and privacy: No credentials are stored in Git, the S3 bucket remains private with versioning enabled, and data transfers use AWS SSM and IAM roles. The platform does not collect user data.
  • Testing and reproducibility: The backend includes 44 automated tests covering ISO week edge cases, spatial filtering, aggregation, F₂ mathematical consistency, and CORS configuration. Terraform allows the infrastructure to be recreated or removed entirely. The project also documents known limitations, including non-independent cell-week observations, weaker F₂ performance at the two-week horizon, reliance on historical rather than live telemetry, satellite coverage gaps, and possible latency under sustained concurrent load.

Key Metrics at a Glance

  • Raw satellite records processed: 548.5 million
  • Unique 1 km cell-weeks after merging: 295.7 million
  • Global deduplication reduction: 46.08%
  • Countries covered: 203
  • Historical coverage: 25 years (2000–2025)
  • Global M₂ MAE reduction: 97.87%
  • Brazil M₂ MAE reduction: 95.88%
  • Brazil F₂ skill score (t+1): +29.47% vs. climatology
  • Global F₂ skill score (t+1): +25.71% vs. climatology
  • Terrestrial forecast grid points: 16,525
  • Forecast horizons: 1–4 weeks (t+1 to t+4)
